figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. A proposed biosynthetic pathway of echinatin in G. inflata and functional characterization of GinF2H and Gin2′OMT. (A) The biosynthetic
pathway of two types of chalcones. 1, echinatin; 2, licochalcone A; 3, 1″-hydroxyl-2′-O-methyllicodione; 4, 2′-O-methyllicodione; 5, 2-
hydroxyliquiritigenin (licodione, ring-opened form); 5′, 2-hydroxyliquiritigenin (flavanone form); 6, liquiritigenin; and 7, isoliquiritigenin. CHS,
chalcone synthase; CHR, chalcone reductase; CHI, chalcone isomerase; F2H, flavanone 2-hydroxylase; 2′OMT, licodione 2′-O-methyltransferase;
and KR, ketoreductase. In the structures of retrochalcones, the phenyl ring attached to the carbonyl group is designated as the A′ ring, and the other
phenyl ring is the B′ ring, though their biosynthetic origins are reversed to normal chalcones. (B) Expression levels of upstream genes in the
transcriptomes of roots and leaves of G. inflata. (C) The catalytic function of GinF2H and Gin2′OMT using 6 as the substrate. The HPLC-UV
chromatograms of enzyme catalytic reaction products were recorded at 300 nm. The substrate was incubated with GinF2H, Gin2′OMT, nicotinamide
adenine dinucleotide (NADH), and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) in 50 mM Tris−HCl buffer (pH 8.0) at 37 °C for 4 h. Compound 4 exists in keto−
enol tautomeric forms and shows two peaks in HPLC analysis.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Functional characterization of ketoreductase. (A) Catalytic functions of GinKR1 and GinKR2 using 4 as the substrate. 8, 7,4′-
dihydroxyflavone; 9, 3″-hydroxyl-2′-O-methyllicodione; and 10, 3-deoxysappanchalcone. △, the products were purified in this study. ∇, the products
were identified by comparing with reference standards. (B) Expression levels of 11 candidate KR genes of G. inflata, which were positively coexpressed
with GinF2H (Pearson’s correlation coefficient, PCC > 0.95), together with GinKR2 (TRINITY_DN470_c0_g2_i2). The expression of each gene is
presented as the transcripts per million of G. inflata transcriptomes. Sample sets 1 and 2 represent two biological replicates. The two positive genes were
labeled in red. TRINITY_DN156_c0_g2_i1 and TRINITY_DN470_c0_g2_i2 were named GinKR1 and GinKR2, respectively. (C) HPLC-UV
chromatograms of the enzyme catalytic reaction products at 300 nm. The reaction mixtures were incubated at 30 °C for 4 h. The dehydrated products 1
and 10 only appeared as tiny peaks due to their poor absorptions at 300 nm. (D) Three groups of one-pot enzymatic catalysis reactions were conducted
to determine the source of retrochalcone carbonyl oxygen. The reaction mixtures were incubated at 20 °C for 24 h. (E) HPLC-UV chromatograms of
reaction products at 300 or 365 nm. (F) (−)-ESI-MS spectra of the products in different groups, showing the [M −H]−ions.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Biosynthesis of echinatin in vivo. Gene expressions of GinKR1 and GinKR2 (A) as well as GinF2H and Gin2′OMT (C) in different groups of
hairy roots of G. inflata and the contents of echinatin and licochalcone A (LCA) (B,D). For all the groups, n = 3, each replicate contains six independent
samples. RNAi, RNA interference; OE, overexpression; EV, empty vector; and ns, nonsignificant. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, and ***p < 0.001, compared
with the empty vector, EV group, by Student’s t-test. (E) De novo biosynthesis of echinatin in tobacco. Phenylalanine ammonia lyase (AtPAL),
cinnamate-4-hydroxylase (AtC4H), and 4-coumarate-CoA ligase (At4CL) are from Arabidopsis thaliana. LC/MS peak areas of products 1, 6, and 7 in
tobacco leaves are shown in the bar graphs (Tables S6 and S7). Data are presented as mean value ± SD (n = 3 biologically independent samples). 1,
echinatin; 6, liquiritigenin; and 7, isoliquiritigenin.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Mechanisms for the selectivity of GinKR1 and GinKR2. (A) The crystal structure of GinKR1 with a resolution of 2.25 Å (PDB ID: 9M3K).
The C-terminal domain is shown in slate, and the N-terminal domain is shown in salmon. (B) Two simulated binding modes of GinKR1 with 4 and
NADH (1″-O-pose and 3″-O-pose). (C) Per-residue contribution to binding energy of GinKR1 with 4 at 1″-O-pose, showing key residues (|
contribution|≥0.5 kcal/mol). (D) The conversion rates of GinKR1 mutants and GinKR2 mutants using 4 as a substrate. Conversion rates represent
the mean of three independent replicates (n = 3). (E) The substrate tunnels of GinKR1 predicted by CAVER 3. The 3″-O-pose tunnel is slate and the
1″-O-pose tunnel is salmon. (F) The substrate tunnels of GinKR2 predicted by CAVER 3. The 3″-O-pose tunnel is slate and the 1″-O-pose tunnel is
salmon.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Distribution of KR1- and KR2-type genes in plants. (A) Discovery of KR1-/KR2-type genes in higher plants based on CNGB search
(https://www. cngb.org). (B) Sequence alignment of the key α10 helix for candidate plant KR genes. The KR1-/KR2-types genes of 13 plant species
are shown. (C) The α10 helix in simulated KR1-/KR2-type enzymes for the 13 species. The structures were simulated by AlphaFold3. (D) Functional
characterization of KR enzymes from three plant species, including CsKR1/2 from C. sativa, HpKR1/2 from H. perforatum, and HlKR1/2 from H.
lupulus. Compound 4 was used as a substrate. The relative ratios of products 3 and 9 are shown as circles. The total conversion rates are given in the
circles as mean of three independent replicates (n = 3). The analytical condition is method C, as shown in Table S10.
